title: Can Spontaneous Time-Translation Symmetry Breaking Be Quantized Without Explicit Branches?
abstract: Can classically branched dynamics associated with spontaneous time-translation-symmetry breaking be quantized without explicitly retaining the branches of the Hamiltonian? We investigate this question using a reduced phase space. formulation in which the Hamiltonian is single-valued, while the critical structure of the classical Legendre map is encoded in a singular, momentum-dependent symplectic geometry. Quantization of the reduced Poisson algebra yields a deformed position-momentum commutator whose singularities determine distinct regular momentum sectors. Using the positive measure induced by the reduced symplectic structure, we identify a bounded central sector and two unbounded outer sectors. In the central sector, states with vanishing mean momentum obey a nonzero lower bound on position uncertainty, subject to the operator-domain assumptions of the representation. We further identify a possible field-theoretic connection with k-essence, where nonlinear scalar-field kinetics can produce finite-velocity degeneracies of the Legendre map. The relationship between the resulting reduced quantum description and branch-matching quantization remains unresolved and requires a comparison of the corresponding Hilbert spaces and operator domains.
summary: This paper tackles the difficult problem of quantizing systems where the classical dynamics are branched due to spontaneous symmetry breaking. It uses a reduced phase-space approach to encode the branching structure into a singular symplectic geometry. The resulting quantum theory predicts specific momentum sectors and suggests connections to k-essence, though the equivalence to full branch quantization remains an open question.
main_problem: The central problem is quantizing classical dynamics associated with spontaneous time-translation symmetry breaking when the underlying Hamiltonian is multivalued (branched), without explicitly tracking these classical branches.
main_result: The reduced quantum description yields a deformed position-momentum commutator, identifying distinct momentum sectors, and suggesting a possible connection to k-essence field theories.
method: The authors employ a reduced phase-space formulation, encoding the classical branching structure into a singular, momentum-dependent symplectic geometry, and then quantizing the resulting reduced Poisson algebra.
model_or_system: The analysis focuses on higher-order velocity-dependent systems whose Lagrangians lead to non-convex kinetic energy terms, causing the canonical momentum-velocity relation to be non-invertible and the Hamiltonian to be branched.
key_observables: Deformed position-momentum commutator, position uncertainty bounds, and the identification of bounded central and unbounded outer momentum sectors.
important_parameters: The singularity structure of the reduced symplectic geometry, and the parameters governing the non-convexity of the kinetic term (e.g., $\alpha, \gamma$ in the representative model).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that a reduced phase-space formulation can capture the essential physics, although the authors note that spectral equivalence with branch-matching quantization is not proven.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the origin of the branched Hamiltonian structure (multiple velocities for one momentum) and show the reduced energy landscape, highlighting outer minima corresponding to finite-velocity ground states.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by introducing the model (Sec. II), quantizing the reduced algebra (Sec. III), and discussing field-theoretic connections (Sec. IV).
why_interesting: While the focus is on general field theory and gravity (hep-th, gr-qc), the methodology of analyzing reduced phase spaces and singular geometries is highly relevant to understanding effective Hamiltonians in complex quantum systems, including those studied in AMO physics.

The figure illustrates how the non-invertibility of the Legendre transformation gives rise to the branched Hamiltonian structure.
